summary: A flickering star is easy to notice. Knowing why it flickers is harder. We've built Project Flipbook to help people explore real SPHEREx infrared observations without mistaking a change in wavelength for a change in the sky. Users can play observations across time, compare shared wavelength coverage, inspect measured spectra and follow catalogue proper motion, with observation dates and source files beside the images. Our starting collection contains 42 FITS files across five fields, including the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855-0714. The viewer supports eight modes and exports animations and measurement tables. Where the data can't support a comparison, it explains the gap. Built for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, Project Flipbook makes the first step of a search more accessible: examining a possible change carefully enough to decide what deserves another look.
details:
Why we built it

Searching for a faint moving object starts with noticing something that changes. But SPHEREx adds a complication: its spatially varying filter means that exposures can sample different wavelengths. A source can appear brighter or fainter even when nothing has changed with time. We didn't want to leave that ambiguity hidden. We wanted a flipbook that helps people ask what an apparent change actually means.

Project Flipbook is Team Overdrive's browser-based tool for exploring that question with real infrared observations. It brings the images and the evidence behind them into the same workspace.

From FITS files to a flipbook

Users can open one of five supplied fields or search by object name or coordinates. The starting collection contains 42 SPHEREx FITS files, with usable pixels in 41 of them. The fields cover Barnard's Star, WISE 0855-0714, Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

Our Python pipeline reads image values, variance and quality flags, together with the zodiacal-light model and spectral coordinates. We mask unusable pixels and register observations onto a common celestial grid. For comparisons between visits, it balances wavelength bins shared by those visits, so that differences in wavelength coverage are considered before interpreting brightness changes. We carry statistical variance through the processing and report missing coverage explicitly.

Eight viewing modes let users blink visits, inspect individual exposures, compare matched wavelengths, examine difference images or follow catalogue motion. Further views include the longest available baseline, false colour and shift-and-stack. Pan, zoom and a wipe comparison help users inspect the frames. We've also included native-pixel aperture measurements with uncertainties and observation dates. Gaia DR3 and CatWISE provide reference overlays when their services are reachable.

You can export GIF or MP4 animations, download measurements as CSV, or share the selected view through a URL. A local flagging tool saves an interesting observation as a JSON note for follow-up. It doesn't send a discovery report.

What makes the approach useful

We've made one central design choice: to make wavelength coverage visible in the comparison itself. We want a striking animation to invite investigation. It needs enough context for us to check it. We've kept observation provenance and measurement limits close to each image. You can check them as you browse. If two visits don't share wavelength coverage, we explain why you can't compare them in that mode.

We've designed this for students and astronomy-curious visitors who want to explore public mission data, as well as reviewers who need to understand what a frame represents. Keyboard controls and accessible measurement tables offer ways to use the viewer beyond watching an animation. Explicitly labelled simulations provide a separate place to explore the interface; failed real-data requests never turn into simulated observations.

Tools and implementation

Our web interface uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Python handles the astronomy processing, using Astropy, NumPy and SciPy, with HTTPX for archive requests and Pillow and FFmpeg for animation export. The repository also lists FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astroquery and Photutils among its dependencies. Docker and Render support deployment, and GitHub Actions runs project checks. We've included a reproducible validation report and an input manifest with file checksums.

Team Overdrive organised the work into four tracks: Malhar Tamhankar on the data pipeline and backend, Akhilesh Rohit Bhosale on image processing, Amrita Patil on spectra and science validation, and team leader Shantanu Pawar on frame stitching, the viewer and demo.

What we can learn from the current data

We're working with sparse coverage in the supplied fields. Barnard's Star has only one visit, and visit counts don't guarantee matching wavelengths for every detector. Bright cores can be masked or saturated. Wavelength balancing is a finite-bin approximation; our pipeline doesn't homogenise the point-spread function or include resampling covariance and calibration systematics in its statistical errors. Catalogue-motion tracking excludes annual parallax.

Project Flipbook supports exploratory inspection. We don't claim a Planet X detection, molecular identification or independently validated astrometry. New archive searches and catalogue overlays depend on external services; the installed fields provide a starting point when those services are unavailable.
